title: 'The Darkness Out There' — Penelope Lively
description: Two teenagers visiting a sweet old neighbour discover she once let a wounded enemy soldier die — and nothing will.
content_html:
Penelope Lively — Context and Background

Penelope Lively (born 1933) is a British novelist and short-story writer whose work frequently explores memory, the past's persistence in the present, and the way people construct narratives to make sense of their experience. The Darkness Out There was published in 1984 in the collection Pack of Cards. It is one of her most celebrated short stories and a staple of GCSE English Literature syllabuses because of its precise, controlled craft and its devastating moral revelation at the centre of an apparently ordinary domestic scene.

The story is set in contemporary rural England — a village with a young people's 'Good Neighbours' group whose teenage members visit elderly residents. This setting draws on a tradition of English rural fiction in which the countryside appears safe, stable, and morally legible. Lively uses this tradition to set up her central act of subversion: Packers End, the local wood that the teenage protagonist Sandra finds sinister, turns out to be less dark than the mind of the seemingly kindly Mrs Rutter.

Key Fact

Sandra fears the wood — Packers End — which she associates with darkness and danger. The story's central irony is that real darkness resides not in the landscape but in Mrs Rutter, the elderly woman who appears to be the embodiment of cosy, harmless domesticity.

Plot and Characters

The story's protagonist is Sandra, a teenage girl whose consciousness we follow throughout. She and a boy named Kerry, who attends the same school, are sent together to visit Mrs Rutter, an elderly woman who lives on the edge of the village. Sandra initially views Kerry with prejudice — she judges him by his appearance and reputation, considering him beneath her socially.

Mrs Rutter is introduced through Sandra's eyes as a quintessentially cosy grandmother figure: pink and white, surrounded by china ornaments, cats, and the warmth of a domestic interior. As they talk and help around the cottage, Mrs Rutter tells them about the wartime crash of a German plane in Packers End. She describes how she and her sister found a wounded German airman — and chose to leave him to die rather than summon help. She tells the story without guilt or remorse, treating it as an anecdote from a distant past. Sandra and Kerry are horrified. Kerry responds with obvious moral clarity; Sandra, who had considered herself superior to Kerry, realises that his moral instincts are sharper than hers were.

The story is a bildungsroman in miniature. Sandra arrives at Mrs Rutter's cottage with a set of easy assumptions: that old ladies are kind, that boys like Kerry are undesirable, and that the world is readable by its surface appearances. She leaves with all three assumptions overturned. The story captures the precise moment of moral awakening — the point at which a young person recognises that the world is more complex, and more dangerous, than they had understood.

Crucially, Sandra's awakening includes a recognition of her own prejudice towards Kerry. She had looked down on him; by the end she sees that his moral response is more instinctive and clear-cut than her own. Lively gives Kerry the dignity of a character who does not need a revelation — he simply knows, immediately, that what Mrs Rutter did was wrong. Sandra's journey is more complicated, which makes it more representative of how most people encounter moral complexity.

Key Themes

The story's central theme is appearance versus reality. Mrs Rutter's cottage, her manner, her appearance — all signal warmth, comfort, and harmlessness. The darkness of the title is not located in Packers End wood (which Sandra dreads) but within Mrs Rutter herself. Lively uses the physical setting of the English countryside — traditionally associated with innocence and safety — to heighten the shock of what Mrs Rutter reveals.

Prejudice and its reversal is equally central. Sandra's dismissal of Kerry — based on his reputation and appearance — is shown to be as misguided as the reader's initial acceptance of Mrs Rutter as a harmless old woman. Lively implicates the reader in Sandra's errors of judgement: we are guided to share her perspective, and when that perspective collapses, we share her discomfort. The story asks readers to examine their own tendency to judge by surface.

Key Fact

Packers End wood is presented as a place of threat and darkness — Sandra is frightened of it. Lively uses this to misdirect the reader's expectations: by establishing an obvious source of danger, she conceals the real source until Mrs Rutter's revelation. The 'darkness out there' turns out to be human, not environmental.

Language, Form, and Structure

Lively uses a close third-person narrator aligned almost entirely with Sandra's perspective. This creates dramatic irony: the reader sees Mrs Rutter's cottage through Sandra's admiring, comfortable eyes, and must re-read that description retroactively once the revelation occurs. Lively's descriptions of the cottage interior — the china, the cats, the warmth — are deliberately cosy precisely because they must be overturned. The language of pastoral comfort is weaponised.

Lively also uses imagery with great precision. The repeated descriptions of the wood — dark, threatening, associated with wartime deaths — and the repeated descriptions of the cottage's warmth create a sustained binary that the story ultimately deconstructs. What is inside (the cottage, Mrs Rutter) is more dangerous than what is outside (the wood).

Lively interrogates gender stereotypes with quiet precision. Sandra's initial dismissal of Kerry reflects gendered assumptions — he is rough, working-class, and male, while she positions herself as more sensitive and socially aware. In fact, Kerry's moral clarity is sharper than Sandra's. Meanwhile, Mrs Rutter subverts the archetype of the gentle, nurturing elderly woman — she is capable of cruelty and feels no remorse about it. Both characters expose the danger of gendered assumptions about moral character.

The story also comments on the construction of femininity: Sandra's initial goals centre on appearance and social standing. By the end, she has moved beyond these preoccupations — the moral shock of Mrs Rutter's revelation forces a more substantive engagement with the world. Lively implies that growing up means learning to see through the surfaces that gender and class construct.

For the exam, this story rewards careful tracking of how Lively constructs and then collapses reader expectations. Note how the setting (pastoral England, cosy cottage) is established to be dismantled, and how Sandra's limited perspective implicates the reader in the same errors of judgement. Link AO2 analysis — the close third-person narration, the binary imagery of wood and cottage — to AO3 context: post-war England, the long shadow of wartime cruelty, and gender stereotypes.
exam_tip_html: In the AQA Telling Tales essay, a strong response on this story will track the story's structure: Lively builds a set of expectations (the frightening wood, the cosy cottage, the superior Sandra, the rough Kerry) precisely in order to subvert them all. Identify this as an AO2 structural technique and explain why it is so effective. Remember that AO3 here includes both wartime history — the German plane, the moral legacy of the war — and gender stereotypes about old women and working-class boys.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lively uses a sustained contrast between the threatening wood (Packers End) and the cosy cottage to misdirect the reader — the real darkness is inside Mrs Rutter, not the landscape.
  • Sandra's coming-of-age is double: she learns that appearances deceive (Mrs Rutter) and that her own prejudices were wrong (Kerry, who has clearer moral instincts than she does).
  • The close third-person narration aligned with Sandra implicates the reader in her errors of judgement, making the revelation more powerful and more personally uncomfortable.

glossary_terms.definition: The technique of establishing an expectation, genre convention, or character type in order to undermine or reverse it, creating surprise and deeper meaning.
Preconceived opinions about a person based on their social group, appearance, or perceived status, not based on individual knowledge.
A coming-of-age narrative in which a young person undergoes a loss of innocence or gains significant moral or emotional understanding.
The gap between how things appear on the surface and what they are in reality, often used in literature to reveal hidden truths or challenge assumptions.
Descriptive writing that appeals to the senses and creates a vivid picture of a place, person, or object.
A situation in which the reader or audience understands more than the characters do, creating tension or a gap between appearance and reality.

practice_questions.text: How does Lively present the theme of appearance versus reality in 'The Darkness Out There'?
practice_questions.marks: Top band (26-30 marks + 4 SPaG): Explores the sustained contrast between the threatening wood and the cosy cottage — and how Lively uses this binary to misdirect the reader. Analyses Mrs Rutter's presentation as a cosy grandmother figure and the shock of her revelation. Discusses Sandra's prejudiced view of Kerry and how this is reversed. Links AO2 (close third-person narration, pastoral imagery, domestic description) to AO3 (postwar England, gender stereotypes, rural England as a site of hidden darkness). Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful analysis with developed argument and context. Upper-mid (16-20): Clear discussion with some analysis. Mid (11-15): Some relevant points. Lower-mid (6-10): Limited response. Lower band (1-5): Simple statements.

practice_questions.text: How does Lively use Sandra's character to explore ideas about prejudice in 'The Darkness Out There'?
practice_questions.marks: Top band (26-30 marks + 4 SPaG): Explores Sandra's dismissal of Kerry — rooted in class and gender prejudice — and its reversal when his moral response to Mrs Rutter's story proves sharper than hers. Analyses Lively's use of close third-person narration to align the reader with Sandra's (flawed) perspective. Discusses the story as a bildungsroman — Sandra's moral awakening as the story's real subject. Links to AO3 context of gender expectations and class assumptions in 1980s England. Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful analysis of character and prejudice. Upper-mid (16-20): Clear argument. Mid (11-15): Some relevant points. Lower-mid (6-10): Limited response. practice_questions.text: How does Lively create a sense of menace in 'The Darkness Out There'?
practice_questions.marks: Top band (26-30 marks + 4 SPaG): Analyses how Lively builds menace through two distinct sources: the overtly threatening Packers End wood (dark, associated with wartime deaths), and the covertly dangerous Mrs Rutter (revealed gradually through her storytelling). Explores how the shift in where menace resides is the story's central structural move. Discusses Lively's use of imagery (domestic warmth vs. outdoor darkness) as a deliberate misdirection. Links to AO3 wartime context. Upper band (21-25): Developed analysis of menace and structure. Upper-mid (16-20): Clear discussion. Mid (11-15): Some points. Lower-mid (6-10): Limited response. Lower band (1-5): Simple statements.

practice_questions.text: How does Lively present ideas about the legacy of the Second World War in 'The Darkness Out There'?
practice_questions.marks: Top band (26-30 marks + 4 SPaG): Explores how the wartime German plane crash in Packers End brings the violence of the past into the apparently peaceful present. Analyses Mrs Rutter's wartime act as a moral failure that she has never processed or repented. Discusses how Lively uses the 'good neighbours' group — a quintessentially peacetime institution — to frame an encounter with wartime cruelty. Links to AO3 context: the Second World War's moral complexities, the treatment of enemy soldiers, and the way communities remember (and misremember) the past. Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful contextual analysis. Upper-mid (16-20): Clear discussion. Mid (11-15): Some relevant points. Lower-mid (6-10): Limited response. Lower band (1-5): Simple statements.

practice_questions.text: How does Lively present Mrs Rutter as a complex character in 'The Darkness Out There'?
practice_questions.marks: Top band (26-30 marks + 4 SPaG): Analyses the deliberate construction of Mrs Rutter as a cosy, harmless grandmother figure — the china, the cats, the pink-and-white appearance — and how this is systematically dismantled. Explores her lack of guilt or remorse as a disturbing form of complexity: she is not a melodramatic villain but someone who committed cruelty and absorbed it into the texture of ordinary life. Links to AO3 context of gender stereotypes and the story's rural English setting. Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful character analysis. Upper-mid (16-20): Clear argument. Mid (11-15): Some points. practice_questions.text: How does Lively use Kerry's character to develop the story's ideas about moral clarity in 'The Darkness Out There'?
practice_questions.marks: Top band (26-30 marks + 4 SPaG): Analyses Kerry as a character who resists easy categorisation — he is dismissed by Sandra as rough and undesirable, but his moral response to Mrs Rutter's story is immediate and unambiguous. Explores how Lively uses Kerry to challenge class and gender prejudices: his instinctive moral clarity contrasts with Sandra's more socially conditioned hesitation. knowledge_checks.q: What does Mrs Rutter reveal she did to the wounded German airman during the war?
options: She reported him to the local authorities immediately
She and her sister left him to die without summoning help
She hid him in her cottage until the war ended
She tried to save him but failed due to her injuries

knowledge_checks.q: At the start of the story, how does Sandra view Kerry?
options: As a close friend she has grown up with in the village
As an admired figure she hopes to impress
As socially beneath her — rough and undesirable
As a rival who challenges her in the Good Neighbours group

knowledge_checks.q: The story's title refers to the 'darkness' that Sandra initially associates with Packers End wood, but which is ultimately shown to reside within Mrs _____.
Lively uses a close _____ narrator, aligned with Sandra's perspective, to make the reader share her errors of judgement.
Match each element of 'The Darkness Out There' to its significance:
right: An obvious source of danger — misdirects the reader from the real threat
A deceptively cosy domestic space — conceals the darkness within its owner
Immediate and clear-cut — exposes Sandra's greater moral confusion by contrast

flashcard_questions.q: Who is the protagonist of 'The Darkness Out There'?
flashcard_questions.a: Sandra — a teenage girl whose moral awakening is the story's subject.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the name of the local wood Sandra fears?
What organisation do Sandra and Kerry belong to when they visit Mrs Rutter?
flashcard_questions.a: A 'Good Neighbours' group for young people helping elderly residents.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Mrs Rutter reveal about the wounded German airman?
flashcard_questions.a: She and her sister found him and left him to die without summoning help.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Mrs Rutter tell the story of the German airman?
flashcard_questions.a: Without guilt or remorse — as an ordinary wartime anecdote.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Sandra's view of Kerry change over the course of the story?
flashcard_questions.a: She realises his moral instincts are clearer than her own — her initial prejudice was wrong.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the term 'appearance versus reality' describe in this story?
flashcard_questions.a: The gap between Mrs Rutter's cosy exterior and her capacity for cruelty.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a bildungsroman, and how does the story fit this form?
flashcard_questions.a: A coming-of-age narrative — Sandra's moral awakening makes this a miniature example.

flashcard_questions.q: What narrative technique does Lively use to align the reader with Sandra's perspective?
flashcard_questions.a: A close third-person narrator that follows Sandra's thoughts and judgements.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is it significant that Packers End is established as threatening early in the story?
flashcard_questions.a: It misdirects the reader — the real danger turns out to be Mrs Rutter, not the wood.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Sandra's initial prejudice against Kerry reflect?
flashcard_questions.a: Class and gender assumptions — she considers him rough and socially beneath her.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Lively's use of domestic imagery (china, cats, warmth) achieve?
flashcard_questions.a: It establishes a cosy surface that is systematically dismantled by the revelation.

flashcard_questions.q: When was 'The Darkness Out There' published?
flashcard_questions.a: 1984, in Penelope Lively's collection Pack of Cards.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'darkness' of the title ultimately revealed to be?
flashcard_questions.a: The cruelty within Mrs Rutter — human darkness, not the landscape.

hero_image_caption: A seemingly safe English village hides a darker past — the warmth of Mrs Rutter's cottage conceals the coldness within.
